title: 22. Interview: Kubernetes
summary: Interview Q&A for Kubernetes — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Kubernetes interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between the control plane and the data plane in Kubernetes?
**Answer:** The control plane (master nodes) is the brain of the cluster — it makes global decisions, stores cluster state, and orchestrates reconciliation. Its components: the **API server** (the front door; all operations go through it via `kubectl` or REST), **etcd** (a Raft-consensus key-value store that is the source of truth for all cluster state — the only stateful control-plane component), the **scheduler** (decides which node each Pod runs on, based on resource requests, affinity, taints), the **controller manager** (runs reconciliation loops — the Deployment controller ensures N replicas, the Node controller evicts Pods from dead nodes, the HPA controller scales replicas based on metrics), and the **cloud controller manager** (integrates with the cloud provider — provisioning load balancers, persistent volumes). The data plane (worker nodes) is where workloads actually run. Each worker node runs the **kubelet** (an agent that talks to the API server, starts/stops containers via the container runtime, reports node status), the **kube-proxy** (manages iptables/IPVS rules that implement Service networking — traffic to a Service's virtual IP is load-balanced across its Pod IPs), and a **container runtime** (containerd, CRI-O, historically Docker). The separation lets the control plane scale to manage thousands of nodes — it is a small set of services, while the data plane scales horizontally with the workload. In a managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS), the cloud provider operates the control plane; you operate only the data plane (worker nodes) and your workloads.
**Visual:**
```
CONTROL PLANE (master, the brain):          DATA PLANE (workers, the muscle):
  +-----------------------+                  +-----------------------+
  | API server (front door|                  | kubelet (agent,       |
  |  for kubectl / REST)  |   watch /        |  starts/stops pods)   |
  | etcd (Raft KV, source |   reconcile      | kube-proxy (iptables  |
  |  of truth)            | <--------------> |  for Service VIP ->   |
  | scheduler (places pods|                  |  pod IPs)             |
  |  on nodes)            |                  | container runtime     |
  | controller manager    |                  |  (containerd/CRI-O)   |
  |  (reconcile loops:    |                  |   pods: order, inv... |
  |  Deployment, Node,HPA)|                  +-----------------------+
  | cloud controller mgr  |                   one per worker node,
  |  (provision LBs, PVs) |                   scales horizontally
  +-----------------------+                   with the workload
   small, managed by cloud provider
   in EKS/GKE/AKS
```

### Q2. What is a Pod, and how does it relate to a Deployment and a Service?
**Answer:** A **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — a co-located group of one or more containers that share network and storage namespaces, scheduled together on one node. Each Pod has its own IP address (in the pod network), and containers in the same Pod share that IP and can communicate via localhost. Pods are ephemeral — they are created, scheduled, and destroyed; when a node dies, its Pods are rescheduled elsewhere with new IPs. You almost never create Pods directly. A **Deployment** is a higher-level object that manages a set of replica Pods. You declare "I want 3 replicas of the order service," and the Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates 3 Pods, monitors them, and replaces any that fail or are evicted. The Deployment also handles rolling updates (replace pods one at a time when the image version changes) and rollbacks. A **Service** is a stable network endpoint that load-balances traffic across the Pods of a Deployment. Because Pods have ephemeral IPs, callers cannot rely on a Pod IP — the Service provides a stable virtual IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name (`order-svc.default.svc.cluster.local`) that resolves to the Service, which load-balances across the ready Pods. So: Deployment manages Pods (lifecycle, scaling, updates); Service exposes Pods (stable networking, load balancing); Pod is the actual running unit. A typical microservice has one Deployment and one Service, plus an Ingress rule for external traffic.
**Visual:**
```
Deployment (order-svc, replicas=3):
  declares: "I want 3 replicas of order:v1"
  manages: rolling updates, rollbacks, replica count
       |
       v
  ReplicaSet (tracks current pod template):
       |
       v
  Pods (3 instances, each with own IP, ephemeral):
    Pod order-svc-1  (IP 10.0.1.5, container order:v1)
    Pod order-svc-2  (IP 10.0.1.6, container order:v1)
    Pod order-svc-3  (IP 10.0.1.7, container order:v1)

Service (order-svc, ClusterIP 10.96.0.5):
  stable virtual IP + DNS name (order-svc.default.svc.cluster.local)
  load-balances across ready pods:
    10.96.0.5 -> 10.0.1.5 or 10.0.1.6 or 10.0.1.7 (round-robin via kube-proxy)
  callers use Service IP/DNS, never pod IPs directly

Ingress (external traffic):
  api.example.com/order -> Service order-svc -> Pods

relationship: Deployment manages Pods (lifecycle); Service exposes Pods (network)
              Pod = running unit, ephemeral IP
```

### Q3. How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) work?
**Answer:** The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler automatically scales the number of Pods in a Deployment (or ReplicaSet) based on observed metrics — most commonly CPU and memory, but also custom metrics (requests-per-second, queue depth) via the custom metrics API. The mechanism: the HPA controller runs a reconciliation loop (default: every 30 seconds). For each HPA target, it queries the metrics server (or custom metrics API) for the current average CPU utilization across all ready Pods of the Deployment. It compares this to the target CPU (e.g., 70%). If current CPU is above target, it computes the desired replica count: `desired = ceil(current_replicas * (current_cpu / target_cpu))`, capped at `maxReplicas`. If below target (and below a lower threshold, typically target/2, to avoid flapping), it computes a lower desired count, floored at `minReplicas`. It then updates the Deployment's `replicas` field, and the Deployment controller creates or terminates Pods to match. The key requirements: (1) each Pod must declare a CPU **request** (so HPA can compute utilization as `usage / request`); without requests, HPA cannot compute CPU percentage. (2) The metrics server must be running (it scrapes CPU/memory from kubelet's cAdvisor). (3) For custom metrics, a custom metrics adapter (Prometheus Adapter, Datadog) must be installed. The HPA's behavior has nuances: it has a stabilization window (default 5 minutes for scale-down) to avoid flapping; it respects `maxReplicas` and `minReplicas`; and for rapid scale-up it can add up to 2x current replicas (or more, for small deployments), but scale-down is conservative. HPA is the primary mechanism for handling load spikes in Kubernetes — combined with Cluster Autoscaler (which adds nodes when Pods are Pending due to insufficient capacity), it gives the elastic scaling that is Kubernetes's headline feature.
**Visual:**
```
HPA spec:
  target CPU: 70%
  minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 10
  deployment: order-svc (current replicas: 3)

HPA controller loop (every 30s):
  (1) query metrics server for avg CPU across ready pods
      pods: order-1 (80%), order-2 (75%), order-3 (70%)
      avg = 75%
  (2) compute desired replicas:
      desired = ceil(3 * (75 / 70)) = ceil(3.21) = 4
  (3) 4 > 3, scale up: update Deployment replicas=4
      Deployment controller creates 1 new pod, scheduler places it
  (4) next loop: avg CPU drops (4 pods sharing load) -> 55%
      55 < 35 (target/2)? no -> no scale-down yet
  (5) after 5 min stabilization window below threshold:
      desired = ceil(4 * (55 / 70)) = ceil(3.14) = 4 -> no change
      or if CPU drops to 30%:
      desired = ceil(4 * (30 / 70)) = ceil(1.71) = 2 -> scale down to 2

requirements:
  - pods must declare CPU request (utilization = usage / request)
  - metrics server running (scrapes kubelet cAdvisor)
  - custom metrics adapter (Prometheus Adapter) for non-CPU metrics

  + Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes when pods Pending (insufficient capacity)
  -> elastic scaling: more pods on same nodes, more nodes when needed
```

### Q4. What is the role of ConfigMaps and Secrets, and how do they differ?
**Answer:** ConfigMaps and Secrets are both Kubernetes objects for injecting non-code configuration into Pods, but they serve different purposes and have different handling. A **ConfigMap** stores non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs — database hostnames, feature flags, log levels, config file contents. Pods consume ConfigMaps as environment variables, command-line arguments, or mounted files (a ConfigMap can be mounted as a directory where each key becomes a file). ConfigMaps are not encrypted — they are stored in etcd in plain text, visible to anyone with `kubectl get configmap`. A **Secret** stores sensitive data — database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates, OAuth tokens. Secrets are structured similarly (key-value pairs) but are stored in etcd base64-encoded (which is encoding, not encryption — but etcd encryption-at-rest can be enabled to actually encrypt them). Secrets can be consumed the same ways as ConfigMaps (env vars, mounted files), and mounted Secret files are written to a tmpfs (RAM-backed filesystem), not disk, so they are not persisted. The right pattern: ConfigMaps for tunables and non-sensitive config; Secrets for credentials. Both can be mounted as files (the cleaner pattern — a config file mounted into the container, hot-updatable when the ConfigMap changes) or as env vars (simpler, but env vars are visible in `kubectl describe pod` and process listings, so less suitable for secrets). For sensitive data that needs rotation, a tool like External Secrets Operator (syncing from AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) is preferred — it manages the Secret object's lifecycle from an external source. The deeper principle is that config and secrets are first-class Kubernetes objects, decoupled from the container image — the same image runs in dev, staging, prod with different ConfigMaps and Secrets mounted.
**Visual:**
```
ConfigMap (non-sensitive config):
  data:
    db_host: "db.internal"
    log_level: "info"
    feature_flag_new_checkout: "true"
  stored in etcd: plain text
  consumed as: env var, mounted file, CLI arg
  visible to: anyone with kubectl get configmap

Secret (sensitive data):
  data:
    db_password: <base64-encoded>
    api_key: <base64-encoded>
    tls.crt: <base64-encoded>
  stored in etcd: base64 (enable encryption-at-rest for real encryption)
  consumed as: env var, mounted file (tmpfs, RAM-backed, not disk)
  visible to: only Pods/service accounts with RBAC permission

mount patterns:
  (1) as file (preferred):
      ConfigMap/Secret -> mounted directory -> container reads file
      + hot-updatable (pod sees changes), structured config
  (2) as env var (simpler):
      ConfigMap/Secret -> container env vars
      - visible in `kubectl describe pod` and process listings
      - not suitable for secrets (use file mount instead)

external secrets (for rotation):
  External Secrets Operator:
    AWS Secrets Manager / Vault -> syncs to -> K8s Secret object
    + rotation handled by external source
    + IAM-controlled access to source
```

### Q5. How does a rolling update work in Kubernetes, and how does it ensure zero downtime?
**Answer:** A rolling update is the strategy Kubernetes uses to update a Deployment to a new version (new image, new env vars, new command) without taking the service down. The mechanism: when you update a Deployment's pod template (e.g., change image from `order:v1` to `order:v2`), the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet for v2 (with 0 replicas initially) and gradually shifts replicas from the old ReplicaSet (v1) to the new one (v2). The parameters `maxSurge` (default 25%) and `maxUnavailable` (default 25%) control the pace: `maxSurge` allows the controller to create new Pods above the desired count (e.g., 4 Pods when desired is 3, to speed up the rollout), and `maxUnavailable` allows some Pods to be unavailable during the update (e.g., down to 2 when desired is 3). The rollout proceeds: create a v2 Pod, wait for it to pass the readiness probe, then terminate a v1 Pod, repeat until all Pods are v2. Zero downtime is achieved through the **readiness probe**: a Pod is added to the Service's endpoints only when its readiness probe passes (the container is ready to serve traffic). So a new v2 Pod does not receive traffic until it is ready, and an old v1 Pod is not terminated (and removed from endpoints) until a replacement is ready. If the rollout goes wrong (v2 Pods fail readiness or crash), the Deployment halts the rollout (because `maxUnavailable` is not exceeded, but new Pods are not becoming ready), and you can `kubectl rollout undo` to revert to v1. For a more conservative rollout, set `maxUnavailable=0` (always keep desired replicas available) and `maxSurge=1` (add one extra Pod at a time). For canary, use a separate Deployment with a small replica count and a Service that load-balances across both Deployments — gradually shift traffic by adjusting replica counts.
**Visual:**
```
Deployment: order-svc, replicas=3, image order:v1 -> order:v2
maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0 (conservative, zero-downtime)

  start:   v1 RS: 3 pods (all ready, in Service endpoints)
           v2 RS: 0 pods

  step 1:  v2 RS: 1 pod (creating)         [maxSurge=1 allows 4 total]
           v1 RS: 3 pods (all still ready)
           endpoints: 3 v1 pods
  step 2:  v2 RS: 1 pod (ready probe passes) -> added to endpoints
           v1 RS: 3 pods
           endpoints: 3 v1 + 1 v2 = 4 pods
  step 3:  terminate 1 v1 pod (removed from endpoints)
           v1 RS: 2 pods, v2 RS: 1 pod
           endpoints: 2 v1 + 1 v2 = 3 pods  [desired maintained]
  step 4:  v2 RS: 2 pods (one creating)
           ... repeat until v1 RS: 0, v2 RS: 3 pods

readiness probe is KEY:
  new pod added to endpoints ONLY when ready probe passes
  old pod removed from endpoints BEFORE termination (with grace period)
  -> traffic never sent to a not-ready or terminating pod -> zero downtime

rollback: kubectl rollout undo (reverts to v1 ReplicaSet)
canary:   separate Deployment with few replicas + shared Service
          shift traffic gradually by adjusting replica counts
```

### Q6. What is the difference between a ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer Service?
**Answer:** These are three Service types in Kubernetes, each exposing the Service differently. **ClusterIP** (the default) exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP — only reachable from within the cluster. This is what you use for internal services (the order service calling the inventory service). The Service gets a virtual IP (e.g., 10.96.0.5) and a DNS name (`inventory-svc.default.svc.cluster.local`), and kube-proxy programs iptables rules so traffic to the ClusterIP is load-balanced across the Pod IPs. ClusterIP is the right choice for the vast majority of services — anything that should not be directly reachable from outside the cluster. **NodePort** exposes the Service on each node's IP at a static port (default range 30000–32767). Traffic to `<any-node-ip>:<nodePort>` is forwarded to the Service, which load-balances to Pods. NodePort is useful for exposing a service to outside the cluster without a cloud load balancer (e.g., in a bare-metal cluster, or for testing), but it has downsides: the port is non-standard (30000+), and if a node dies, that node's IP is no longer valid (you need an external load balancer in front of the nodes to handle node failure). **LoadBalancer** (cloud-managed) provisions a cloud load balancer (AWS ELB/NLB, GCP TCP Load Balancer, Azure Load Balancer) that forwards external traffic to the Service. The cloud controller manager handles provisioning; the Service gets an external IP (the LB's). LoadBalancer is the right choice for exposing a service to the internet on a cloud-managed Kubernetes — but each LoadBalancer Service costs money (one cloud LB per Service), so for many public services, an **Ingress** (one LB for many services, routed by hostname/path) is preferred. In practice: ClusterIP for internal services, Ingress (backed by one LoadBalancer Service) for HTTP services exposed to the internet, LoadBalancer for non-HTTP services (TCP, UDP).
**Visual:**
```
ClusterIP (default, internal):
  Service gets virtual IP (10.96.0.5) + DNS name
  reachable ONLY from within the cluster
  use for: internal services (order -> inventory)
  + free, simple
  - not reachable from outside

NodePort (exposes on each node):
  Service exposed on <node-ip>:30000-32767 (static port per service)
  traffic to any node's IP at that port -> Service -> Pods
  use for: bare-metal clusters, testing
  + no cloud LB needed
  - non-standard port, node failure needs external LB

LoadBalancer (cloud-provisioned):
  cloud controller provisions a cloud LB (ELB/NLB)
  Service gets external IP (the LB's)
  use for: non-HTTP services exposed to internet (TCP/UDP)
  + standard ports, handles node failure
  - costs money (one cloud LB per Service)

Ingress (preferred for HTTP):
  one LoadBalancer Service backs an Ingress Controller (nginx, ALB)
  Ingress rules route by hostname/path to multiple Services
  use for: HTTP services exposed to internet
  + one LB for many services (cheaper)
  + hostname/path-based routing, TLS termination
  - HTTP/HTTPS only (use LoadBalancer for TCP)

typical setup:
  external HTTP -> Ingress (1 LB) -> Service A (ClusterIP) -> Pods
                                  -> Service B (ClusterIP) -> Pods
  internal svc-to-svc -> ClusterIP -> Pods
```

### Q7. What happens when a node fails in a Kubernetes cluster?
**Answer:** When a node fails (hardware crash, network partition, kubelet stops), Kubernetes detects it and reschedules the affected Pods to healthy nodes, automatically restoring the desired state. The mechanism: the **Node controller** (in the control plane) monitors node health via the kubelet's periodic heartbeats (default: every 10 seconds, with a 40-second grace period before marking the node `NotReady`). After a node is `NotReady` for 5 minutes (the `pod-eviction-timeout`, configurable), the Node controller evicts the Pods — it deletes the Pod objects from etcd, which signals the Deployment controller that the desired replica count is not met, and the Deployment controller creates replacement Pods on healthy nodes (via the scheduler). Until the eviction timeout, the Pods on the failed node are in `Terminating` state but still counted as replicas — this delay is to avoid premature eviction during transient network blips. Stateful workloads (StatefulSet, databases) need special handling: the Pod is bound to its persistent volume, and Kubernetes does not allow two Pods with the same identity to run simultaneously — so the eviction waits for the volume to detach, which can take minutes. For stateless workloads (the common case), eviction and rescheduling happen within seconds of the timeout. The impact on traffic: the Service's endpoints are updated (the kube-proxy on each node updates iptables rules) to remove the failed node's Pods, so new traffic goes only to healthy Pods. During the window between node failure and rescheduling, capacity is reduced (fewer replicas serving), which can cause latency spikes under load — this is why running multiple replicas across multiple nodes is important (a single replica on a failed node means downtime until rescheduling completes). For mission-critical workloads, use Pod anti-affinity to spread replicas across nodes, PodDisruptionBudgets to prevent too many simultaneous evictions, and topology spread constraints to balance replicas across zones.
**Visual:**
```
node-2 fails at t=0 (hardware crash, kubelet stops heartbeating)

  t=0:    node-2 stops sending heartbeats
  t=40s:  node controller marks node-2 "NotReady"
          pods on node-2 still counted as replicas (Terminating state)
          -> Service endpoints still include them? No:
             kube-proxy updates iptables to remove dead pod IPs
             -> traffic stops going to node-2's pods
             -> capacity reduced (fewer replicas serving)
  t=5min: pod-eviction-timeout expires
          node controller evicts pods on node-2 (deletes pod objects)
          Deployment controller notices replicas < desired
          -> creates replacement pods on healthy nodes (node-1, node-3)
          -> scheduler places them, kubelet starts them
          -> readiness probe passes -> added to Service endpoints
  t=5min+10s: capacity restored, full replica count serving

  stateless workload: eviction + rescheduling within seconds of timeout
  stateful workload (StatefulSet, DB):
    pod bound to persistent volume
    cannot run two pods with same identity simultaneously
    -> eviction waits for volume to detach (can take minutes)

  best practices to minimize impact:
    - multiple replicas (avoid single-replica single-node failure)
    - pod anti-affinity: spread replicas across nodes
    - PodDisruptionBudget: prevent too many simultaneous evictions
    - topology spread constraints: balance across zones
    - multi-zone cluster: a zone failure does not take down all replicas
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your team is migrating from a VM-based deployment (one service per VM, autoscaled by an AWS Auto Scaling Group) to Kubernetes. What changes, and what stays the same?
**Answer:** The migration from VMs to Kubernetes changes the unit of deployment, the scaling mechanism, and the operational model — but the application architecture (services, APIs, data) stays the same. **What changes.** (1) **Unit of deployment**: from a VM (an entire OS instance per service) to a Pod (a container or small group of containers, many per node). You pack many Pods onto each node, sharing the node's OS kernel — higher density, lower overhead. (2) **Scaling mechanism**: from an ASG (adds VMs based on CloudWatch metrics, takes minutes to provision a new VM) to HPA + Cluster Autoscaler (adds Pods in seconds when CPU exceeds threshold; adds nodes when Pods are Pending due to insufficient capacity). Scaling is faster and more granular. (3) **Networking**: from VM IP addresses (stable, registered in service discovery) to Service virtual IPs + DNS (stable abstraction over ephemeral Pod IPs). The kube-proxy handles load balancing across Pods; you no longer need an external load balancer per service for internal calls. (4) **Configuration**: from VM user-data scripts and SSH-based deploys to ConfigMaps, Secrets, and `kubectl apply`. The deployment becomes declarative YAML, version-controlled. (5) **Updates**: from ASG instance replacement (slow, all-or-nothing) to rolling updates (Pod-by-Pod, with readiness checks, zero downtime). **What stays the same.** The application code, the service boundaries, the databases, the inter-service communication patterns (HTTP/gRPC, eventing). The migration is largely a deployment-and-operations change, not an application rewrite. The teams that struggle are usually the ones that try to lift-and-shift VM assumptions (long-running processes, SSH debugging, OS-level dependencies) — Kubernetes works best when applications are designed for it (stateless, configurable via env vars, health-checkable, gracefully shutdownable).
**Visual:**
```
VM-based (before):                     Kubernetes (after):
  +----------------------+              +----------------------+
  | VM: order-svc        |              | node-1 (shared OS)  |
  |  - full OS           |              |  Pod: order-1       |
  |  - one service       |              |  Pod: order-2       |
  |  - autoscaled via ASG|              |  Pod: inventory-1   |
  +----------------------+              +----------------------+
  +----------------------+              +----------------------+
  | VM: inventory-svc    |              | node-2 (shared OS)  |
  |  - full OS           |              |  Pod: order-3       |
  |  - one service       |              |  Pod: inventory-2   |
  |  - autoscaled via ASG|              +----------------------+
  +----------------------+              shared kernel, higher density

changes:
  unit: VM (full OS) -> Pod (container, many per node)
  scaling: ASG adds VMs (minutes) -> HPA adds Pods (seconds) + Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes
  networking: VM IPs -> Service virtual IPs + DNS (kube-proxy load-balances)
  config: user-data scripts -> ConfigMaps/Secrets (declarative YAML)
  updates: ASG instance replacement -> rolling updates (Pod-by-Pod, zero downtime)

stays the same:
  application code, service boundaries, databases, inter-svc communication
  (HTTP/gRPC, eventing)

struggle points:
  long-running processes (Pods are ephemeral, design for restarts)
  SSH debugging (no SSH in K8s; use kubectl logs, exec, port-forward)
  OS-level dependencies (bake into image, not the node)
```

### Q2. Your Pods are stuck in `Pending` state. How do you debug this?
**Answer:** Pods stuck in `Pending` means the scheduler could not place them on a node. Debugging follows a systematic checklist. **(1) `kubectl describe pod <name>`** — look at the `Events` section at the bottom. The most common reasons: `FailedScheduling` with a message like `0/5 nodes are available: 5 Insufficient cpu` (not enough CPU capacity), `5 Insufficient memory`, `5 node(s) didn't match node selector`, `5 node(s) had taints that the pod didn't tolerate`, `5 MatchNodeSelector`. The message tells you the constraint that is failing. **(2) Insufficient resources.** If the message is "Insufficient cpu/memory," check the Pod's resource requests (`resources.requests.cpu`, `resources.requests.memory`) against the cluster's available capacity. If the cluster is full, either reduce the Pod's requests, or add nodes (Cluster Autoscaler should do this automatically if enabled — check that it is running). Also check for "stranded" resources: nodes that are `NotReady` but still holding allocated resources, or Pods in `Terminating` state that are not actually terminating (force-delete them). **(3) Node selector / affinity / taints.** If the message mentions selectors or taints, check the Pod's `nodeSelector`, `nodeAffinity`, `tolerations`, and the nodes' labels and taints. A common mistake: a Pod with `nodeSelector: disktype=ssd` but no nodes have that label. **(4) PersistentVolumeClaims.** If the Pod uses a PVC, check `kubectl get pvc` — if the PVC is `Pending`, the Pod cannot schedule (it needs the volume attached). The PVC may be Pending because the StorageClass cannot provision (e.g., AWS EBS unavailable in the region). **(5) Image pull issues.** If the Pod is `Pending` with `ImagePullBackOff`, it is not a scheduling problem but an image problem — check the image name, registry credentials (imagePullSecrets), and that the image exists. **(6) ResourceQuota / LimitRange.** If a namespace has a ResourceQuota, a Pod may be Pending because the quota is exceeded. Check `kubectl get resourcequota`. The systematic approach: describe the Pod, read the event message, address the specific constraint.
**Visual:**
```
Pod stuck in Pending: debug checklist

  (1) kubectl describe pod <name> -> read Events section
      common messages:
        "0/5 nodes available: 5 Insufficient cpu"      -> not enough capacity
        "5 Insufficient memory"
        "5 node(s) didn't match node selector"         -> selector/affinity issue
        "5 node(s) had taints that the pod didn't tolerate"
        "5 MatchNodeSelector"
        "persistentvolumeclaim ... not found"          -> PVC issue

  (2) Insufficient resources:
      check pod's resources.requests.cpu/memory
      check cluster capacity: kubectl describe nodes (Allocatable vs Allocated)
      if full: reduce requests, OR add nodes (Cluster Autoscaler)
      check for stranded resources: NotReady nodes, stuck Terminating pods

  (3) Node selector / affinity / taints:
      check pod's nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, tolerations
      check nodes' labels (kubectl get nodes --show-labels) and taints
      common mistake: nodeSelector: disktype=ssd but no nodes have label

  (4) PersistentVolumeClaims:
      kubectl get pvc -> if Pending, StorageClass cannot provision
      check EBS availability, StorageClass config

  (5) Image pull issues (Pending -> ImagePullBackOff):
      check image name, registry credentials (imagePullSecrets), image exists

  (6) ResourceQuota / LimitRange:
      kubectl get resourcequota -> namespace quota exceeded?

  systematic: describe pod -> read event -> address specific constraint
```

### Q3. You deployed a new version of a service, and 50% of requests are now failing. How do you roll back, and how do you prevent this next time?
**Answer:** Roll back immediately, then investigate, then prevent recurrence. **(1) Roll back.** `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>` reverts the Deployment to the previous ReplicaSet (the previous pod template). This is fast (seconds) — Kubernetes creates new Pods with the old version, waits for them to be ready, then terminates the new version's Pods. You can also roll back to a specific revision with `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=N`. If the rollout is mid-progress (some new, some old), `kubectl rollout pause` stops it, then `undo` reverts. **(2) Investigate.** Why did 50% fail? Check the new Pods' logs (`kubectl logs <pod>`), events (`kubectl describe pod`), and metrics (the new Pods' error rate, latency, restart count). Common causes: a bug in the new version, a missing ConfigMap/Secret, a schema mismatch with the database, a dependency on a new env var that was not set, a readiness probe that passes but the service is not actually healthy (liveness probe might catch it). The 50% failure (not 100%) suggests the rollout was partial — some new Pods are serving and failing, old Pods are still serving and succeeding. **(3) Prevent recurrence.** (a) **Canary deployment**: instead of rolling all replicas at once, deploy the new version to a small canary (1–2 replicas with a separate Service or with traffic splitting via Istio/Linkerd), watch metrics for 5–15 minutes, then ramp to 100% if healthy. This catches the bug at 5% impact, not 50%. (b) **Stronger readiness probe**: the readiness probe should check that the service can actually serve (e.g., a `/health` endpoint that queries the database), not just that the port is open — a weak probe lets unhealthy Pods into the endpoints. (c) **Automated rollback**: tools like Argo Rollouts or Flagger can automatically roll back when metrics (error rate, latency) regress during a rollout. (d) **Pre-prod testing**: the bug should have been caught in staging — invest in integration tests and staging that mirrors prod.
**Visual:**
```
50% of requests failing after new version deploy:

  IMMEDIATE: kubectl rollout undo deployment/order-svc
    -> reverts to previous ReplicaSet (old version)
    -> Kubernetes creates old-version pods, waits ready, terminates new pods
    -> seconds to revert
    alternative: kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=N (specific revision)
    if mid-progress: kubectl rollout pause, then undo

  INVESTIGATE (after rollback):
    kubectl logs <new-version-pod>          -> error messages
    kubectl describe pod <new-version-pod>  -> events
    metrics: new pods' error rate, latency, restart count
    common causes: bug, missing ConfigMap/Secret, schema mismatch,
                   missing env var, weak readiness probe

  PREVENT RECURRENCE:
    (a) canary deployment:
        deploy new version to 1-2 canary replicas (separate Service or
        traffic split via Istio/Linkerd)
        watch metrics 5-15 min -> ramp to 100% if healthy
        catches bug at 5% impact, not 50%
    (b) stronger readiness probe:
        /health endpoint that checks DB connection, downstream deps
        not just "port is open"
    (c) automated rollback:
        Argo Rollouts / Flagger auto-revert on metric regression
    (d) pre-prod testing:
        integration tests in staging that mirrors prod
```

### Q4. Your cluster's control plane is run by a cloud provider (EKS/GKE/AKS), but your worker nodes keep running out of CPU. How do you handle autoscaling?
**Answer:** Worker-node autoscaling is handled by the **Cluster Autoscaler** (or Karpenter, a newer AWS-native alternative), which watches for Pods stuck in `Pending` due to insufficient resources and adds nodes to the cluster. The mechanism: when the scheduler cannot place a Pod (because no node has enough free CPU/memory), the Pod stays in `Pending` with a `FailedScheduling` event. The Cluster Autoscaler notices these Pending Pods, computes what instance types would fit (based on the Pod's resource requests and the node group's instance types), and requests new nodes from the cloud provider (an ASG in AWS, a MIG in GCP). Once the new node joins the cluster (1–3 minutes), the scheduler places the Pending Pods. When nodes are underutilized (Pods could be rescheduled elsewhere), the Cluster Autoscaler drains and removes them to save cost. **Configuration.** (1) Define node groups (ASGs) with multiple instance types (e.g., m5.large, m5.xlarge, c5.large) so the autoscaler can pick the best fit. (2) Set min and max node counts (min for baseline capacity, max for cost control). (3) Enable the Cluster Autoscaler (it runs as a Deployment in the cluster, or use Karpenter on AWS). (4) Make sure Pods have accurate resource requests — the autoscaler scales based on requests, not actual usage, so under-requesting leads to over-packing and performance issues. **Karpenter (AWS).** AWS's Karpenter is a newer, faster alternative to Cluster Autoscaler — it provisions nodes directly (no ASG), picks instance types based on Pending Pod requirements, and can scale up in seconds (vs Cluster Autoscaler's minutes). It also handles spot instances natively for cost savings. **Combined with HPA.** The full scaling stack: HPA scales Pods based on CPU (seconds), Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter scales nodes when Pods are Pending (minutes). Together they give elastic scaling — Pod-level responsiveness with node-level capacity. **Cost considerations.** Set max node counts to prevent runaway cost; use spot instances for stateless, interruptible workloads; use `cluster-autoscaler`'s `--scale-down-delay-after-add` and `--scale-down-unneeded-time` to control how quickly underutilized nodes are removed.
**Visual:**
```
worker nodes running out of CPU:

  HPA scales pods based on CPU (seconds):
    CPU > 70% -> HPA increases Deployment replicas
    new pods created, but Pending if no node has capacity

  Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter scales nodes (minutes):
    watches for Pending pods (FailedScheduling: Insufficient cpu)
    computes instance types that fit pod requests
    requests new nodes from cloud provider (ASG in AWS, MIG in GCP)
    new node joins cluster (1-3 min) -> scheduler places Pending pods

    when nodes underutilized:
      drains pods (reschedules elsewhere), removes nodes (save cost)

  configuration:
    (1) node groups with multiple instance types (m5.large, c5.large...)
    (2) min/max node counts (min=baseline, max=cost control)
    (3) Cluster Autoscaler as Deployment in cluster, OR Karpenter (AWS)
    (4) accurate pod resource requests (autoscaler scales on requests)

  Karpenter (AWS, newer, faster):
    provisions nodes directly (no ASG), picks instance type per pod req
    scales up in seconds (vs Cluster Autoscaler's minutes)
    native spot instance support

  full scaling stack:
    HPA (pods, seconds) + Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter (nodes, minutes)
    -> elastic scaling: pod-level responsiveness + node-level capacity

  cost controls: max node count, spot instances for stateless workloads
```

### Q5. You need to run a database (PostgreSQL) on Kubernetes. What special considerations apply, compared to running a stateless service?
**Answer:** Stateful workloads (databases, message queues, caches with persistence) on Kubernetes require special handling that stateless services do not. **(1) Persistent storage.** The database's data must survive Pod restarts — it cannot live in the container's ephemeral filesystem. Use a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) backed by a cloud volume (EBS, Persistent Disk, Azure Disk) or networked storage (NFS, Ceph). The PVC is mounted into the Pod, and data persists across Pod restarts. For high availability, use a volume that supports multi-attach (ReadWriteMany) only if the database supports it (most do not — PostgreSQL is single-writer). **(2) StatefulSet, not Deployment.** Use a StatefulSet, which gives Pods stable identities (`postgres-0`, `postgres-1`), stable network names, and ordered startup/shutdown. This matters for databases with primary/replica replication — `postgres-0` is the primary, `postgres-1` is the replica, and the order is deterministic. A Deployment gives Pods random names and unordered startup, which does not work for stateful clusters. **(3) Stable network identity.** Each StatefulSet Pod has a stable DNS name (`postgres-0.postgres.default.svc.cluster.local`), so replicas can find the primary by name — they do not need to discover it dynamically. **(4) Headless Service.** A headless Service (clusterIP: None) returns the Pod IPs directly (via DNS A records), so callers can target specific Pods (the primary) rather than load-balancing across all. **(5) Pod anti-affinity and topology spread.** Spread database Pods across nodes and zones — a single node or zone failure should not take down both primary and replica. Use `podAntiAffinity` (require different nodes) and `topologySpreadConstraints` (across zones). **(6) Backup and disaster recovery.** Automated backups (e.g., Wal-G for PostgreSQL, backing up to S3) and Point-In-Time-Recovery (PITR) are essential — Kubernetes does not back up your database for you. **(7) Consider a managed database instead.** For most teams, running a database on Kubernetes is more pain than benefit — managed databases (RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora) handle backups, replication, failover, and patching for you. Run stateless services on Kubernetes; run databases on managed services unless you have a specific reason to do otherwise (e.g., a multi-tenant DBaaS product).
**Visual:**
```
stateless service (Deployment):
  +----------------+
  | Pod (ephemeral)|
  |  no data       |
  |  random name   |
  |  any node      |
  +----------------+
  restart = new pod, no data loss (no data to lose)
  scale = add pods anywhere

database (StatefulSet):
  +----------------+     +-----------------+
  | Pod postgres-0 |     | PVC (EBS vol)   |
  |  stable name   |<--->|  survives pod   |
  |  stable DNS    |     |  restarts       |
  |  ordered start |     +-----------------+
  +----------------+
  +----------------+     +-----------------+
  | Pod postgres-1 |     | PVC (EBS vol)   |
  |  (replica)     |<--->|                 |
  +----------------+     +-----------------+

  considerations:
    (1) PersistentVolumeClaim (cloud volume, data survives restarts)
    (2) StatefulSet (stable identity, ordered startup)
    (3) stable DNS (postgres-0.svc, replicas find primary)
    (4) headless Service (clusterIP: None, returns pod IPs)
    (5) podAntiAffinity + topologySpreadConstraints (across nodes, zones)
    (6) automated backups (Wal-G to S3), PITR
    (7) CONSIDER MANAGED DB INSTEAD (RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora)
        unless specific reason to run on K8s (DBaaS product)
```

### Q6. You have 50 microservices, each with its own Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, and HPA YAML files — 300+ files total. How do you manage this sprawl?
**Answer:** YAML sprawl is the most common operational pain in mature Kubernetes deployments. Three layers of tooling address it, in increasing sophistication. **(1) Helm (template-and-package).** Write a Helm chart per service (or one parameterized chart for all services) — a template with values for image, replica count, env vars, etc. Each service is a `values.yaml` that instantiates the chart. `helm install` renders the templates and applies them. Helm reduces 6 files per service to 1 chart + 1 values file, and changes are versioned as chart releases (rollback with `helm rollback`). Trade-off: Helm templates use Go templating, which can become complex (logic in templates is a code smell). **(2) Kustomize (overlay-based, no templating).** Define a base YAML manifest per service, then overlays (`kustomization.yaml`) for dev/staging/prod that patch the base (different images, replica counts, env vars). Kustomize is built into `kubectl`, no templating language — pure YAML patching. Trade-off: less powerful than Helm for parameterization, but simpler and more transparent. **(3) GitOps (ArgoCD, Flux).** Store all YAML (or Helm charts, or Kustomize bases) in a Git repo. ArgoCD/Flux runs in the cluster, watches the repo, and automatically applies changes — the Git repo is the source of truth, and the cluster reconciles to it. This gives: audit trail (every change is a Git commit), review process (PRs), rollback (`git revert`), and drift detection (ArgoCD shows when the cluster diverges from Git). GitOps is the standard for mature Kubernetes operations — it replaces `kubectl apply` from CI with a pull-based model where the cluster pulls its desired state from Git. **For 50 services.** The right stack is: a parameterized Helm chart (or Kustomize base) for the common service shape, a `values.yaml` per service for the specifics, all stored in Git, deployed via ArgoCD. New services are added by dropping a `values.yaml` — the chart, manifests, and deployment are reused. This reduces 300 files to 50 values files plus one shared chart.
**Visual:**
```
50 services x 6 files each = 300+ YAML files (sprawl)

  (1) Helm (template-and-package):
      one chart per service (or one parameterized chart for all):
        templates/deployment.yaml   (Go template)
        templates/service.yaml
        templates/configmap.yaml
        values.yaml                 (per-service: image, replicas, env)
      helm install -> renders templates -> applies
      + 6 files per service -> 1 chart + 1 values file
      + versioned releases (helm rollback)
      - Go templating can become complex (logic in templates)

  (2) Kustomize (overlay-based, no templating):
      base/manifests.yaml (base YAML per service)
      overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml (patches: dev image, replicas)
      overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml (patches: prod image, replicas)
      kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
      + built into kubectl, no templating language, pure YAML
      - less powerful than Helm for parameterization

  (3) GitOps (ArgoCD, Flux) -- the standard for mature ops:
      all YAML (or Helm charts) in Git repo
      ArgoCD/Flux runs in cluster, watches repo, auto-applies
      + audit trail (every change is a Git commit)
      + review process (PRs)
      + rollback (git revert)
      + drift detection (ArgoCD shows cluster vs Git divergence)
      + pull-based (cluster pulls desired state, no kubectl from CI)

  for 50 services:
    one parameterized Helm chart (common service shape)
    + values.yaml per service (specifics)
    + all in Git
    + ArgoCD deploys
    = 50 values files + 1 shared chart (not 300 files)
    new service = drop a values.yaml (chart, manifests, deploy reused)
```

### Q7. Your team wants to deploy to Kubernetes but is worried about vendor lock-in (EKS vs GKE vs AKS vs self-hosted). How do you minimize it?
**Answer:** Kubernetes itself is portable (it is open-source, CNCF-graduated, runs the same on any cloud), but the ecosystem around it can couple you to a specific cloud. Minimizing lock-in means choosing portable abstractions and avoiding cloud-specific ones where possible. **(1) Use a managed control plane (EKS, GKE, AKS), do not self-host.** Self-hosting the control plane (kubeadm, kops) is operationally expensive (etcd HA, certificate management, control-plane upgrades) and gives you no real portability benefit — the control plane API is the same on managed. Use managed; the control plane is portable (your manifests work on any managed K8s). **(2) Avoid cloud-specific CRDs and annotations.** Some tools (like the AWS Load Balancer Controller, GCP's Compute Persistent Disk CSI) use cloud-specific annotations or Custom Resource Definitions. If you use them heavily, migrating means rewriting those. Prefer portable alternatives where possible: the standard Ingress (with nginx ingress controller) instead of cloud-specific ALB ingress; the standard PersistentVolumeClaim with a portable StorageClass. **(3) Container registry.** Use a registry that supports replication (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, Quay) or push to multiple cloud registries (ECR, GCR, ACR) via CI. Avoid baking cloud-specific image references into manifests. **(4) Secrets and config.** If you use External Secrets Operator with a cloud-specific source (AWS Secrets Manager), migrating to another cloud means changing the source (to Vault, or the other cloud's secret manager). Use External Secrets with a portable source (Vault) if portability is critical. **(5) CI/CD and GitOps.** Use ArgoCD/Flux (portable) rather than cloud-specific deploy tools (AWS CodeDeploy, GCP Cloud Deploy). **(6) Accept some cloud coupling for cost savings.** Using cloud-native services (ALB for ingress, EBS for storage) is often cheaper and more integrated than portable alternatives. The pragmatic stance: be portable where it is cheap (manifests, Helm charts, GitOps), and accept coupling where the cost of portability is high (storage classes, load balancers) — but document the coupled points so a future migration is scoped. For most teams, full portability is not worth the cost; a documented set of cloud-coupled points is the right balance.
**Visual:**
```
minimizing K8s vendor lock-in:

  PORTABLE (use freely, same on any cloud):
    - manifests (Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret)
    - Helm charts, Kustomize bases
    - standard Ingress (with nginx ingress controller)
    - standard PVC (with portable StorageClass, e.g., Rook/Ceph)
    - container images (push to multiple registries via CI)
    - ArgoCD / Flux (GitOps, portable)
    - Prometheus, Jaeger, Grafana (observability, portable)
    - managed control plane (EKS/GKE/AKS - API is the same)

  CLOUD-COUPLED (document, accept for cost/integration):
    - AWS Load Balancer Controller (ALB annotations)
    - cloud-specific StorageClass (EBS, PD, Azure Disk)
    - External Secrets with AWS Secrets Manager (source-specific)
    - cloud-specific node groups (ASG, MIG, VMSS)
    - cloud IAM integration (IRSA on AWS, Workload Identity on GCP)

  PRAGMATIC STANCE:
    be portable where cheap (manifests, charts, GitOps)
    accept coupling where portability cost is high (storage, LBs)
    document coupled points -> future migration is scoped

  ANTI-PATTERNS (maximize lock-in unnecessarily):
    - self-hosted control plane (operational cost, no portability benefit)
    - cloud-specific deploy tools (CodeDeploy, Cloud Deploy)
    - cloud-specific CRDs scattered through manifests
    - single cloud registry with no replication
```
